ns_flame.name: Candle Flame
ns_flame.question: What shapes a laminar diffusion flame and makes its tip flicker?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: What shapes a laminar diffusion flame and makes its tip flicker?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: A simplified flame model: an advected mixture variable Z with a prescribed source velocity at the wick, a temperature proxy T(Z) that peaks on the stoichiometric surface, and buoyancy proportional to it. The teardrop shape and the tip flicker come from that coupling.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Move Z_st from 0.08 to 0.30: the luminous sheet moves relative to the fuel core.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: The flame-tip height and its flicker spectrum.
more: Lower the buoyancy to make the flame shorter and steadier.

layers.title: Physical explanation
layers.text:
A candle does not burn like a campfire log; it is a laminar diffusion flame. Heat melts and vaporises wax at the wick, the fuel vapour rises, and oxygen from the surrounding air diffuses inward to meet it. Fuel and oxidiser can only react where they coexist in the right ratio, so the burning is confined to a thin sheet — the stoichiometric surface — that wraps around the rising fuel like a sock.

All the heat is released on that sheet. It makes the gas there much lighter, so buoyancy shoots it upward; the rising column drags in fresh air at the base, which feeds the flame and anchors it to the wick. That same buoyant acceleration is unstable: a ring of vorticity forms and sheds periodically, pinching the flame and making the tip flicker at a few cycles a second. The slender teardrop, the steady anchoring, and the flicker all fall out of this fuel-meets-air-plus-buoyancy picture. This scene reproduces it with a simplified model — a mixture variable, a prescribed wick inflow, a temperature proxy and buoyancy — without chemistry or heat release.

layers.title: Equations, symbols and assumptions
layers.text:
• Z — mixture variable: 1 in the fuel from the wick, 0 in the ambient air; advected and diffused, with a model decay away from the source (not conserved)
• Z = Z_st — the stoichiometric surface where fuel and air meet in burning proportion (the sheet)
• T(Z) — temperature: peaks on the sheet (fast 'Burke–Schumann' chemistry) and falls either side
• f_b = β·T·ŷ — Boussinesq buoyancy: the hot sheet is light and rises
• 𝒟∇²Z — diffusion of the mixture, which sets the thickness of the luminous zone

layers.title: Initial and boundary conditions (this preset)
layers.ic: Still, cool air everywhere (mixture variable Z = 0); the wick begins releasing fuel at t = 0.
layers.bc: A thin inlet at the wick with a prescribed upward velocity (Z → 1) on the floor; a free-slip floor, side walls with lateral damping, an open top through which the hot products leave, and a decay of Z away from the source (model terms, see the checks).

layers.title: Numerical method, checks and limitations
layers.text: The incompressible projection solver carries a mixture variable Z (Z = 1 in the fuel leaving the wick, Z = 0 in the surrounding air) with a prescribed inflow velocity at the wick, lateral damping of the flow and a decay of Z away from the source. In the Burke–Schumann picture the flame sheet sits on Z = Z_st, where the temperature proxy T(Z) (a tent function of Z) peaks; that proxy drives the Boussinesq buoyancy and is the field rendered.
layers.checks: Qualitative demonstration. The model prescribes the wick velocity, damps the flow laterally, and uses a temperature proxy, not chemistry or heat release; it is not a combustion simulation.

layers.title: References
items: Peters, N. (2000). Turbulent Combustion. Cambridge (mixture fraction, Burke–Schumann limit).

buoyancy.label: Heat-release buoyancy
buoyancy.help: How strongly the temperature proxy T(Z) lifts the gas. Stronger buoyancy draws the fuel up faster, keeping the flame slender and steady.

zst.label: Stoichiometric mixture  Z_st
zst.help: The fuel/air ratio at which the flame sheet sits. The luminous sheet is the Z = Z_st surface; a larger value pulls it tighter to the fuel core.

source.label: Wick width
source.help: Width of the fuel vapour leaving the wick. A thin wick gives a slender flame.

confinement.label: Vorticity confinement
confinement.help: Sharpens the small eddies that make the flame tip lick and wander (a modelling knob).

viscosity.label: Viscosity
viscosity.help: Kinematic viscosity ν — how 'thick' the fluid is. Lower → finer, more chaotic structures; higher → smoother, damped flow.

resolution.label: Resolution
resolution.help: Grid resolution. It changes the grid, and with it whatever a scene ties to the grid: the elapsed convective time in the wind tunnel, the Rayleigh number in the convection scenes, the grain size in the rock, the extent of the blast box. The derived readouts say what moved for this experiment; runs at different resolutions are comparable only where they say so.

duration.label: Duration (×)
duration.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
